R2:interp.title: Extracting physics from learned models to fix simulators (Goodfire discovery pattern)
R2:interp.summary: Symbolic regression on GNN internals recovers force laws that generalize out of distribution better than the network itself. MeshGraphNets learn cloth simulation 1-2 orders of magnitude faster than the simulator they were trained on. Goodfire distilled SAE features of an Alzheimer's model into a simple fragment-length classifier (small cohort, wide confidence intervals). The extrapolation: learn real cloth and wet-friction dynamics, then interpret them into better simulator models. It is the only route that attacks model-form error directly. Unproven for cloth, and it still needs real measurements. Rating: speculative, highest ceiling.

R2:interp.title: Capacity, interference and memorization analysis for long-tail skills
R2:interp.summary: Huang et al. (listed by Goodfire) show smaller models spend neurons on frequent tasks and lose rare, complex ones through gradient interference; larger OLMo models retain them. GEN-0 reports ossification at 1B parameters and a phase transition at 7B. Goodfire's loss-curvature method separates memorization from generalization in the weights. Together these give a mechanistic reason long-tail items like wine glasses are dropped by small policies, and a guide for model sizing and data mixtures. Untested on robot policies. Rating: low-medium.

roots.question: Can scientific paper reviews (maybe specifically ML, DL, data-driven papers) be automated with highly scoped, small subagents following the AISLE model: many open-source models, since they have different blind spots, with tasks scoped to known failure modes like biases, factual reproduction errors, 'do these authors/papers exist' errors and overclaims, including building the suggested experiments and variations and running them on GPUs? Is compute a major blocker at some level, could a shit ton of GPU parallelism fix it?

What's actually stopping general purpose robot hands from reliably doing stuff like folding laundry or loading a dishwasher? Is it the lack of real-world manipulation data, the hardware (sensors, actuators, tactile feedback), or the sim-to-real gap? Is that a major blocker at some level, and could it be fixed by running millions of simulated robots in parallel on a shit ton of GPUs?

Why can't we predict earthquakes days or hours in advance? Is it fundamentally chaotic physics that no model can get around, or is it mostly a data problem with too few sensors and too few big quakes to learn from? Could training huge foundation models on decades of global seismic waveforms, GPS strain and fault simulations with a shit ton of GPU parallelism actually get somewhere, or is compute not the blocker at all?

What actually stops us from autoformalizing most of published math into Lean? Is it gaps in Mathlib coverage, the step of translating informal proofs where authors skip things that are 'obvious', or something deeper about how mathematicians write? The Lean kernel is a free and perfect verifier, so this looks like one of the few domains where brute-force search can't fool itself. Could you split every paper into tiny lemma-sized subgoals and throw many different open-source prover models at each one in parallel, with each model scoped to a known failure mode like wrong definitions, mismatched conventions or silently strengthened hypotheses? Is compute a major blocker at some level, and could a shit ton of GPU parallelism fix it, or is the real bottleneck checking that the formal statement means the same thing as the English one?

What limits general-purpose robot manipulation right now? Is it lack of real-world data, the sim-to-real gap, or hardware like hands and tactile sensors? If you can already run millions of simulated environments in parallel on GPUs with heavy domain randomization, why can't you brute-force a policy that folds laundry or ties knots and then transfers to a real robot? Is contact and deformable-object physics the wall that no amount of compute gets you over because the simulator itself is wrong in ways you can't randomize away? Or could a shit ton of GPU parallelism plus a small fleet of real robots that keeps correcting the simulator close the loop?

plan.question: Can an equation distilled from a sparse neural residual, trained on real cloth motion capture, beat the best hand-designed aerodynamic fix on unseen speeds?
plan.hypothesis: Law from a sparse residual network can cut cloth error on fast unseen motions by at least 15% versus best hand-designed drag.

compute_axis.quantity: Fraction of the real-data volume used in the planted-law positive control (data size, not compute; the file says the experiment is not compute-bound)

held_fixed: Same 500-evaluation CMA-ES budget for every model (B1, B2, candidate)
Splits made strictly by recording, never by window
Same real recorded corner trajectories drive the simulator
Pre-registered thresholds (15% on speed split, 2% on negative control)

predictions.if_lever: Distilled law has at least 15% lower median error than best hand-designed drag on 32 fast recordings, interval excluding zero, no worse than black-box.
predictions.if_not: Distilled law roughly equals the hand-designed baseline (rediscovering textbook drag), or black-box residual fails to beat it; more or denser data needed, not compute.
predictions.decision_rule: Primary claim holds if candidate median error is >=15% lower than B2 on the speed split over 32 test recordings, paired-bootstrap 95% CI excludes 0, and candidate is no worse than B3; same functional form selected in >=4 of 5 seeds.
predictions.noise_rule: Paired bootstrap 95% CI over test recordings; 5 seeds per primary split; form stability in >=4 of 5 seeds; negative controls (no planted term, time-shuffled targets) must improve held-out error by less than 2%.
predictions.expected_why: The file states no expected outcome; it lists four outcomes and notes the work is limited by data and validation, not FLOPs.

plan.compute_tested_why: The file says the experiment is limited by data and validation, not FLOPs (NOT COMPUTE-BOUND). The only varied quantity is data volume in the synthetic control, which parallel compute does not buy.
plan.scored_against: Held-out recorded marker positions, scored by the dataset paper's mass-weighted mean marker distance (eq. 1) on held-out speed, motion, size and fabric splits, compared with baseline B2 (best hand-designed aerodynamic term, same tuning budget).

checks: Loader unit test: error of a recording against itself is 0; rigid non-moving sheet gives a sanity upper bound
Positive control: planted quadratic normal drag and an angle-of-attack drag term recovered (sympy-equivalent, coefficients within 20%) in >=4 of 5 seeds at 100% data, with 0.1 mm and 1 mm noise
Mismatched-internals control with different mesh resolution and bending stiffness
Negative control: no planted term, and real data with residual targets shuffled in time; improvement under 2%
Speed scaling: term roughly proportional to v^2; predicted about 8x larger on fast recordings (5-11x)
Density scaling: per-mass effect about 1/areal density, about 2.9x larger on polyester
Dissipation: f.v <= 0 over observed range and invariant to normal sign flip
Baseline sanity: B2 in-sample error within about 1.5x of published under 1 cm
Optional external replication on Blanco-Mulero fling data with frozen form

phases.what: Synthetic controls: planted and no-law, 5 seeds; data-size curve 25/50/100% with 3 seeds; mismatched internals; about 19 runs x 2 GPU-hr; Gate G2

gate.else: Stop or rescope: positive control failing at 100% real-data scale would mean 12-20 markers per cloth are too sparse to extract a force law

phases.what: Real-data sweep: 41 residual training runs, 8 split configs x 3 models CMA-ES fits, PySR on host CPUs; Option A 4x A6000 (default) or Option B 8x A100; scale by measured GPU-hr per run / 4; if projected total exceeds $1,000 cut fabric folds to 2 seeds first

pick.title: Capacity, interference and memorization analysis for long-tail skills

plan.option_title: Capacity, interference and memorization analysis (model sizing for the long tail)
plan.question: Do small robot policies drop rare skills because of too few samples, no spare capacity, overwriting by common tasks, or narrow memorized storage?
plan.hypothesis: Rare-task success of small behaviour-cloning policies improves with width beyond a task-difficulty baseline, as in the OLMo result [huang], because common-task updates interfere with rare skills.

compute_axis.quantity: Policy hidden width (MLP width in Meta-World stage; parameters from about 5K to about 9M)

held_fixed: 100K Adam steps at batch 1,024 for every width (Meta-World)
Same task identities, with task-to-rank order re-drawn per seed
Same expert demonstrations (5,000 successful episodes per task)

predictions.if_lever: Gap between common-task and rare-task success shrinks as width grows when tasks are unevenly sampled, beyond the uniform-sampling baseline, and matched single-task models succeed.
predictions.if_not: The width-by-frequency interaction is near zero (under 5 points per width doubling), so long-tail failure is just too few rare-task samples.
predictions.decision_rule: H1 refuted if the interaction CI includes 0 and its point estimate is under 5 points per width doubling.
predictions.noise_rule: Logistic mixed model success ~ log2(width) x log(pi) + (1|task) + (1|seed), hierarchical bootstrap over seeds then tasks, 3 seeds, tasks pooled into frequency quintiles, hypotheses pre-registered.
predictions.expected_why: The file gives no expected outcome; the plan is built so that each of H1 to H5 can fail, and prior evidence is only OLMo and LLM.

plan.compute_tested_why: Width (parameter count) is swept over 7 values with step count held fixed, with a 5x longer training control at small widths.
plan.scored_against: Per-task rollout success in simulation (Meta-World fresh positions, LIBERO-90 rollouts) with Wilson intervals, compared with uniform sampling (beta = 0), single-task matched models, tuned plain-sum training and random-direction edits.

anchor.what: Reproduce the Huang et al. toy linear model: retained encoder features must match the analytic top-N utility set (Theorem 3) at every width [huang_html].
anchor.tolerance: At least 95% of features agree at every width; gradient norms respect the Theorem 4 bound

checks: Stage 0 toy must match theory before GPU spend (gate G0)
Metric unit tests: identical tasks cosine about 1, disjoint blocks about 0, M2 matches first-order -eta*g_rare*g_common within 5%
K-FAC subspace compared with exact Gauss-Newton eigendecomposition at width 32
G1: expert success at least 95% on fresh positions; width-2048 uniform policy at least 80% mean success
G2: width-512 uniform head at least 30% mean success with at least 30 of 90 tasks at 50% or more
G3: random-label task must lose performance before any real task under low-curvature removal
Ablating units assigned to task k must drop rollout success more than ablating random units (10 tasks per width)
Group projection must lower M1/M2 interference and raise rare-task success
Hypotheses H1-H5 and analysis script committed before the full sweeps

records.card: **opt-12-capacity-memorization · Capacity, interference and memorization analysis for long-tail skills.** R2 · interp · random pick · compute tested: yes · plan expects: unsure · halted: cost record broken **Question.** Do small robot policies drop rare skills because of too few samples, no spare capacity, overwriting by common tasks, or narrow memorized storage? **What is known.** Huang et al. show smaller OLMo models (4M to 4B parameters) allocate neurons to frequent tasks and show more gradient interference; no robot-policy test exists per the option text. Whether width-by-task-frequency effects and low-curvature storage of rare skills appear in robot behaviour-cloning policies; two prior-art searches were not completed. **Hypothesis.** Rare-task success of small behaviour-cloning policies improves with width beyond a task-difficulty baseline, as in the OLMo result [huang], because common-task updates interfere with rare skills. **If compute is the lever.** Gap between common-task and rare-task success shrinks as width grows when tasks are unevenly sampled, beyond the uniform-sampling baseline, and matched single-task models succeed. **If not.** The width-by-frequency interaction is near zero (under 5 points per width doubling), so long-tail failure is just too few rare-task samples. **Test.** Sweep MLP and transformer-head widths on Meta-World MT50 and LIBERO-90 with power-law task frequencies, using controls for scarcity, under-training and tuned baselines, then probe curvature edits to see whether width, rebalancing or protecting rare gradients helps rare skills. *Compute axis.* Policy hidden width (MLP width in Meta-World stage; parameters from about 5K to about 9M): 32–2,048 hidden units, 7 levels. Closest prior: not on this axis. *Restructuring.* none. **Check first.** Reproduce the Huang et al. toy linear model: retained encoder features must match the analytic top-N utility set (Theorem 3) at every width [huang_html]. Tolerance: At least 95% of features agree at every width; gradient norms respect the Theorem 4 bound. **Would not show.** Simulation only, policies up to about 10^7 parameters; a null result would not refute GEN-0's 1B-7B claims. Scripted unimodal experts and a frozen encoder in Stage 2 may hide effects present with human data. *Cost.* Plans $211 of the $1,000 budget, leaving $789.
